3.0.0.en: This chapter begins by confirming the continuation of the boy's service, which he had begun from his childhood. This service was of course under the supervision of "Eli" the priest, who guided him as his disciple. The inspired text indicates here that visions, prophetic dreams and God's speaking with His people were very rare, because of the people's sins and spiritual dryness, and also the evil of the priests, as we saw in the person of the two sons of "Eli the priest." But God does not leave Himself without a witness, so He spoke to the boy Samuel and prepared him to lead the people. In every generation there is one who fears God and proclaims His voice, like the prophet Moses among the people who went astray and worshipped the golden calf, and Pope Athanasius who preserved the faith despite the deviation of many.

3.1.0.en: In this time, when the word of the Lord had become precious, "Eli" was sitting in his tent, very near to the tabernacle of meeting, and specifically opposite it, as was the custom of the priests' dwellings. This verse indicates that his sight was very weak and that his eyes could not see as they had, which hindered his service.

3.2.0.en: The lamp of God: this is the golden lampstand with its seven lamps, which was lit throughout the night and put out in the early morning at the time of dawn.

3.2.1.en: Of course no one spent the night in the Holy Place, the Holy of Holies or the temple of the Lord. Samuel used to dwell in a tent next to the tent of "Eli" the priest, where he could serve him and hasten to him when he heard his voice, and what is mentioned here is a figure for the nearness of Samuel's tent to the tabernacle of meeting. At about the time of dawn the boy Samuel heard a voice calling him by name. He did not know whose voice it was, but he supposed it was the voice of Eli the priest, so he answered with his voice, before going to him, "Here I am," as one of us might say to another who calls him ("Yes" or "Present"). We notice that the Bible mentions that Eli lay down in his place (v. 2), while Samuel lay down in the temple of the Lord, to declare that righteous Samuel felt the awe and greatness of the house of the Lord, whereas Eli lay down in his body and did not feel the fear of God.

3.3.0.en: Samuel hurried and ran to "Eli" the priest and said to him: Yes, I am here as you called me. Eli answered him that he had not called him, and told him to go back and sleep.

3.4.0.en: What had happened was repeated a second time, and Eli the priest sent the boy Samuel back to sleep. Verse 7 makes clear to us that the boy Samuel could not tell that this voice was God, for this was the first time God spoke with him, especially as he was still young. There is a great difference between Samuel's not knowing the voice of God and Hophni and Phinehas's not knowing God because of their evils. But when it happened the third time, the priest, old in days, understood by his spiritual sense that it was God who was speaking with the boy.

3.5.0.en: So he sent him back a third time to his place, but this time he gave him new advice, telling him that when he heard this voice again, he should answer the One who spoke with the phrase "Speak, Lord, for Your servant hears." The boy Samuel went, obedient to his teacher, with a courage rarely found in a small boy.

3.5.1.en: God allowed the righteous boy Samuel to learn how to recognize the voice of God from the hand of Eli, the negligent high priest, so that Samuel might learn humility and learning from his elders, which is what boys and youths need in every generation.

3.5.2.en: Samuel was a righteous boy who loved God, and "Eli" was condemned before God for his shortcoming, his laxity and his lack of decisiveness in depriving his sons as recompense for their evil. Yet God used "Eli the priest" to guide Samuel and inform him that the voice he heard was the voice of God. How much more, then, the priesthood of the New Testament, which works by the Spirit! So, beloved, do not neglect the counsel of your spiritual father when you find it hard to understand God's purposes in your life.

3.6.0.en: The Lord came and stood: that is, He appeared in the form of a person who can be seen.

3.6.1.en: The first three times were calls only, but this time it was accompanied by a divine appearance, as happened to other persons in the Old Testament. When the Lord began His speech, Samuel answered with the words of "Eli": "Speak, for Your servant hears."

3.7.0.en: God began to speak, declaring to the boy Samuel the first prophecy he received as a prophet from God. The subject of this prophecy was momentous and grave, for God described His work as going to be so severe that people's ears could not bear it, and the expression "both ears will tingle" is a figure for the severity and fear that will strike the people. These events will be like the roar of thunder or the frightening sound that ears dread and fear.

3.8.0.en: On the day appointed for this matter God will carry out all that He spoke and all that the prophet told "Eli" of punishment (ch. 2:27-33), and when He begins He will not delay or stop until He has fulfilled all His previous words.

3.9.0.en: Here God explains to the boy Samuel what he had of course not heard in the conversation of the man of God with "Eli." From God's speech here with Samuel we draw more than one spiritual meaning:

3.9.1.en: 1- God wants to speak with every pure and clean heart, and rank does not matter to Him, even if he is a boy.

3.9.2.en: 2- By this speech God wanted to calm Samuel's heart so that he would not stumble at the severity of the coming events, and would understand that all this is God's just judgment.

3.9.3.en: 3- God declares to Samuel and to us that although He is long-suffering, He does not excuse the wicked, licentious one from his guilt, and this makes a person examine himself and take account of his steps.

3.9.4.en: 4- God wanted to declare to Samuel, and afterward to "Eli" the priest, that Samuel is the one chosen as prophet, judge and priest for Israel.

3.10.0.en: The Lord concludes His speech with Samuel with hard words: that He will not accept from Eli and his family any sacrifices of atonement or any offering to appease Him, because they persist in their faults. Their worship is outward, and God does not accept the worship of the wicked who do not want to leave their sins, but whoever is weak and falls into sin, God accepts him if he repents.

3.11.s.en: (2) Telling Eli, and Samuel's declaration as a prophet of the Lord

3.11.0.en: The vision was at about dawn, after which Samuel settled on his bed for a short time before morning. We do not know whether he slept or remained astonished and meditating on what he had heard and on his first vision. At morning he began his daily work and opened the doors of the tabernacle of meeting in preparation for the morning services. He had made a decision in his heart not to tell "Eli" what he had seen and heard, because of his fear for him on account of the hardness of the news, and this shows the tenderness of his feelings.

3.12.0.en: May God do so to you, and more also: may God be angry with you and punish you.

3.12.1.en: Eli wanted to know what God had said to Samuel, so he summoned him, and when the boy came before him he commanded him to tell him all that had happened and not to leave out a single word, or else God would bring down His wrath.

3.13.0.en: Before Eli's insistence and his threat of God's punishment, Samuel confessed everything and hid nothing from him. As for "Eli," he submitted to God's punishment in weakness and defeat, though it would have been more fitting for him to offer repentance with tears before God and to punish his two sons, and then God would have relented of the evil that He was going to do.

3.14.0.en: After that Samuel grew in age, mind, wisdom and spirituality, and he was with the Lord, so the Lord was with him and gave him the spirit of prophecy, so that everything he uttered came to pass. All the Israelites in all the land from one end to the other (Dan the farthest north, and Beersheba the farthest south) knew, and it became known among them and they became certain, as time passed, that God had chosen Samuel as a prophet and a man of His.

3.15.0.en: This chapter began by affirming the fact that the word of God was precious and rare (v. 1), but at the end of the chapter, with the presence of the spiritual man, Samuel, the chapter ends with the words "the Lord appeared again." The beginning of the Lord's return was by appearing to Samuel when he was a boy, followed afterward by other visions and other works of standing by His people and choosing "David" afterward as their king.

3.15.1.en: When afflictions come upon you, or you hear the voice of God in the Bible or from the mouth of your father of confession, hasten to repent and change your life, leaving your evils, and you will receive God's mercies, for He is a tender Father who warns you so that you may repent and does not want to punish you.

3.15.2.en: The defeat of Israel before the Philistines

4.0.0.en: Aphek: a city in the south of the land of the Jews where the children of Israel fought the Philistines this time and then again in the days of Saul (1 Sam 29:1). Ebenezer: it lies southeast of Aphek.

4.0.1.en: The first part of this verse is a continuation of the last two verses of the previous chapter. After the people knew that Samuel was a prophet trusted by God, his word came to all Israel, meaning that he became a father, prophet and guide to the people in all their affairs. Despite this, no one consulted him before going out to fight the Philistines, because they did not care to hear the voice of God, so God abandoned them in the battle because of their pride and their sins, as will appear later.

4.0.2.en: The second part of this verse tells us that Israel went out to fight the Philistines. We do not know the motive or reason behind this war, but it is known that enmity had long been entrenched between the two peoples and they had many wars. The prophet Samuel mentions the place where the Israelite army encamped, whose name is "Ebenezer," a place that Samuel himself gave this name (ch. 7:12), and the Philistines were drawn up before it at a place named "Aphek."

4.1.0.en: Of the army: of the men drawn up in line, the soldiers. The field: the battleground or the field of combat.

4.1.1.en: The war broke out between the two sides, and this was the first battle. This round ended in a defeat for the people of the children of Israel, in which about four thousand men died. Although this number is large, it cannot be compared with the greater loss in the second round of the war.

4.2.0.en: The camp: what is meant here is the army's encampment.

4.2.1.en: In ancient times war continued throughout the day, and at the end of the day each side returned to its camp until the next day, to resume the war or end it by surrender. At the end of the first day the leaders of the people gathered in their camp and discussed the matter ... why was there defeat, and why did the enemies triumph over them, and what is the secret of God's abandoning them? An idea for victory came to their minds, which was to bring the ark of the covenant, which represented the divine presence in the midst of the people, thinking that the presence of the ark would give them victory, not knowing that their defeat was because of their evil, their lack of repentance and the wickedness of their priests. For the Lord's blessing on a person is connected with his striving and repentance, and not with merely keeping blessed things.

4.2.2.en: Formal worship without repentance is of no benefit, just as the Jews in the days of Jeremiah relied on the presence of the temple in Jerusalem and their worship in it while immersed in sins, so Babylon attacked them and burned Jerusalem and the temple, and the temple did them no good at all. Likewise today someone wears a golden cross and does not believe in its power, and so he benefits nothing.

4.3.0.en: In a new haste and error, the people did not consult God about the ark leaving the place He had set apart for it in the Holy of Holies, but carried it and moved it from the tent. Of course the priests accompanied the ark and carried it, among them Hophni and Phinehas, the sons of Eli the priest. When the ark reached the camp of the fighting people, all the men shouted with a great shout, so that the earth shook under their feet from the roar of the shouting and joy, but this shout was from the mouths and not from the heart, so it did them no good.

4.4.0.en: The Philistines heard the sound of the great shout, and in their astonishment at the roar of the shouting they perhaps sent some of their men to the camp of the Israelites as spies, and learned that this shout was because of the arrival of the "ark of the covenant into the camp of Israel." When the Philistines knew this their hearts melted with fear, and they said to themselves, Woe to us, for nothing awaits us but defeat, since the God of Israel has come to the place of battle. This is something we are not accustomed to from the Israelites in all our wars with them, that they should bring their God with them and show such zeal in fighting.

4.5.0.en: As fear continued within the ranks of the Philistines, they reviewed the power of the God of Israel, who was always with His people, and how He gave them victory over Egypt, the greatest kingdom in the world in that time, through the ten plagues. They remember well how God drowned the whole army of Egypt in the Red Sea when Israel went out into the wilderness. This fear was of course enough for them to withdraw from the battlefield, but because the Lord's will was something else, and He wanted His just judgment to be carried out, He put something else in the heart of the Philistines. Their fear drove them to take courage and fight bravely with all their strength so as not to be enslaved to the people of Israel, and the expression "as they have been to you" goes back to the fact that the Philistines considered the Hebrews a foreign people whose land this was not, and when they came in the early days from Abraham, Isaac and Jacob they were a small band whom the Philistines looked on with contempt as slaves.

4.6.0.en: The Philistines fought with strength and intensity, and the Lord did not support Israel, so their defeat was very great, for thirty thousand of the Jews fell and the rest fled. In this place also both Hophni and Phinehas, the sons of Eli the priest, died, and the Lord fulfilled His just judgment and His prophecy concerning them. As for the ark of the covenant, the Israelites left it at the time of their defeat and the Philistines took it with them. The psychological loss of the ark of the Lord was greater than all their slain, for the ark represented their pride and their strength, and its absence was a clear sign of God's anger against them and their loss of spiritual blessing.

4.6.1.en: Do not rely on your superficial worship of God while excusing some sins, for the only solution is repentance, or else God will abandon you and you will lose every blessing and be defeated before Satan.

4.7.0.en: Eli the priest was very anxious about the ark of the covenant's leaving the tent and going to the camp of battle, not knowing whether this was right or wrong. He could not wait in his house, but went out and sat by the road waiting for any news that might come to him. A man from the ranks of the army, of the tribe of Benjamin, had come back from the battle to Shiloh, the place of the tabernacle, with dust on his head and his clothes torn, and he told them of the defeat. Then crying and wailing went up over the loss of the war and over the slain men, and the cry of the women rose and covered the whole place.

4.8.0.en: Eli heard these loud, sorrowful sounds, and was alarmed and asked about the matter, so the Benjamite man came to him and told him all that had happened.

4.9.0.en: His eyes were set: they had lost sight completely.

4.9.1.en: "Eli" the priest was nearly a hundred years old and had completely lost his sight when the man told him that he had fled from the battle, that Israel was defeated before the Philistines, that his two sons Hophni and Phinehas were dead, and that they had lost the ark of the covenant.

4.10.0.en: Eli listened to all this painful news, very sorrowful to his soul, including the report of the death of his two sons, but when he learned that the matter had reached the loss of the ark of the covenant, he lost his balance and his body fell backward, and because of the weight of his body he fell to the ground, so his neck was broken and he died at once, for his old age also hastened the matter. Samuel, the writer of the book, mentions that "Eli" had judged and ruled his people for forty years.

4.11.0.en: Labor: the contractions, pains and signs of childbirth.

4.11.1.en: The wife of Phinehas, the son of Eli, was about to give birth, and when she heard the whole set of bad news at once, unexpected contractions came that hastened the birth. At the time of delivery the women around her noticed the paleness of her face and her sharp decline, as if it were the hour of her death. The women wanted to encourage her that she had borne a male son, but because of her intense grief, her sickness and her decline she could not answer, and her heart was not gladdened by anything.

4.12.0.en: Ichabod: a name meaning where is the glory, or the glory has departed.

4.12.1.en: The last words spoken by Phinehas's wife, in her intense grief and despair, were that she called her son's name Ichabod, because the glory had departed with the loss of the ark of God's covenant and the death of her father-in-law and her husband. This shows her faith in God, for she grieved over the loss of the ark more than over the loss of her husband and her father-in-law.

4.12.2.en: The loss of the ark was a discipline for the children of Israel, in that God would not dwell among them because of their evils, and it was a discipline for the Philistines for their cruelty and their many assaults on the people of God, for the ark troubled them and struck them with diseases, as will appear later.

4.12.3.en: When you hear sorrowful news, do not stand alone, but hasten to God to support you, and speak with your spiritual father and with your loved ones so that your heart may be at rest, then think positively, that is, do what you are able to do to solve the problem. The First Book of Samuel. The ark and its strikes on the Philistines
